steelman: A book club's identity is partly formed around shared reading culture; if the organiser — who sets the group's tone and book selections — visibly abandons physical books, members who treat the paper-book ritual as central to the experience may interpret this as a signal that the group is changing character. Under social identity theory, even one anchor member's visible shift can prompt gradual exit among the most tradition-oriented participants. Some members might also worry that future book selections will skew toward e-book-only titles or that the discussion dynamic will change. A community-management consultant reviewing a membership drop might include 'check whether a visible cultural signal from leadership alienated a cohort' on a diagnostic checklist.
mechanism_if_any: Social identity / cultural drift: organiser's device choice signals a group-culture shift, alienating tradition-oriented members. However, this mechanism is speculative, operates over months-to-years, and requires members to perceive and react to the organiser's private device choice — there is no structural pathway by which the organiser's personal reading device affects other members' ability or motivation to attend a meeting.
notes: The distractor is cleanly non-causal. The organiser's private reading device has no structural effect on members' ability to attend. The abruptness of the drop (same month as venue change) alone rules out a slow cultural-drift mechanism. A senior practitioner presented with a concurrent venue move to a transit-inaccessible location would not put the organiser's e-reader on a root-cause checklist. The seed is well-constructed: the xbase temporal anchor ('the drop happened the same month') implicitly forecloses the slow-drift mechanism without needing an explicit statement. No repair needed.
